Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.

articles.title: Gaze World Model
articles.summary: Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods…
articles.abstract: Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts. Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode. This relationship is subtle, however, since an event far across the frame may produce only a slight movement of the person's head or eyes. We therefore introduce the Gaze World Model (GWM), which co-trains latent scene prediction with person-conditioned gaze supervision on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; in our ablations, the latent prediction objective improves both shift detection and gaze localization. Given a video clip and the person's head box, GWM estimates gaze locations and detects gaze shifts in the observed clip, and forecasts future gaze and shifts from predicted scene features. To train and evaluate these tasks, we augment VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay with event-level gaze-shift annotations. GWM achieves state-of-the-art shift detection on these benchmarks, about 10 points higher in four-class AP than the strongest baseline, while remaining comparable to the strongest image-based models in gaze target estimation, and outperforms the compared baselines on future gaze localization and shift forecasting.

articles.title: POISE: Curvature-Aware Critic Regularization for Smooth Actor-Critic Control
articles.summary: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the…
articles.abstract: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature. The same gradient change, however, moves the critic's preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further shows that the shift's curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by $5.9\times$ on average ($4.5\times$ geometric mean), compared with $2.2\times$ ($1.9\times$) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks. Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

articles.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
articles.summary: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created…
articles.abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

articles.title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
articles.summary: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods…
articles.abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

articles.title: Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks
articles.summary: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the…
articles.abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.

articles.title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
articles.summary: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath…
articles.abstract: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.

articles.title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication
articles.summary: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under…
articles.abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.

articles.title: A Generative AI Agent to Emulate Interactive Human-driven Vehicles for Automated Driving Testing in Urban Areas
articles.summary: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical…
articles.abstract: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical interactions involving high collision risk for the following reasons: they often assume full observability, overlooking interactions arising from occlusion. Driving styles are mainly characterized by vehicle maneuvers, limiting the diversity of safety-critical interaction behaviors. Moreover, learning signals from safety-critical interactions can be diluted by non-critical driving behaviors. To address these issues, we propose a generative AI agent to emulate interactive HDVs. The agent incorporates field-of-view modeling to account for driver visibility under occlusion and characterizes the interaction process using five metrics spanning its initial, intermediate, and final stages. It automatically learns diverse interaction styles through a dynamic mixture-of-experts network. Through residual reinforcement learning, the agent further refines generated trajectories to match the real-world distributions of safety-critical interaction characteristics. Experiments on the INTERACTION dataset show that our method reduces Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) by 39.9\%--87.1\% across five interaction characteristics compared with a state-of-the-art baseline. Our method achieves greater improvements of up to 87.1\% in final-stage interaction metrics, suggesting that it can reduce error accumulation in long-horizon trajectory generation. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component, particularly highlighting the importance of residual refinement. Generalization experiments show that our method approaches the performance of full training on unseen intersections with only one epoch of fine-tuning.

articles.title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
articles.summary: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models…
articles.abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.

articles.title: AGL-SKILL: Coding Harnesses as Agentic Optimizers
articles.summary: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and…
articles.abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and prompts that provide task-related information or guide the behaviour of the model. Skills, being textual in nature, present themselves as another editable surface to be optimized; current methods have improved on handcrafting and one-shot generation by treating skill development as an iterative process, using score-driven search to tweak and improve performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of the agents themselves as optimizers: across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. More broadly, this shows the capability of agents to do such work and to refine their own behaviour to provide task-specific context, as long as they are given a metric to measure against.

articles.title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators
articles.summary: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited…
articles.abstract: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

articles.title: SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures
articles.summary: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale…
articles.abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.

articles.title: VISOR: A Vision-Language Selector for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
articles.summary: Recent time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast a distribution over futures, and multimodal time-series (TS) forecasting further exploits other modalities to improve forecasting accuracy.…
articles.abstract: Recent time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast a distribution over futures, and multimodal time-series (TS) forecasting further exploits other modalities to improve forecasting accuracy. However, existing works have two limitations: 1) TSFMs reduce the predictive distribution to its median or mean, flattening diverse futures into a calm line, and 2) multimodal TS forecasting models incorporate text into the forecaster through TS-language alignment, which is substantially weaker than vision-language alignment. To address these limitations, we propose the VIsion-language SelectOR (VISOR), a multimodal TS forecasting framework that selects one plausible future instead of averaging across candidates, leveraging the alignment capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to select the most suitable candidate based on textual information. VISOR consists of two components: 1) a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures, and 2) a VLM selector that reads the candidates as a single chart image and selects one based on the text. To avoid overly calm forecasting paths, we train the selector with a shape-aware target that evaluates each candidate based on both point-wise error and path shape. Across three benchmarks covering ten datasets, VISOR achieves the best average ranking in both point and volatility errors compared with TSFMs and multimodal TS forecasting models. Code: https://github.com/seunghan96/VISOR.

articles.title: SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering
articles.summary: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires…
articles.abstract: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM plan it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.

articles.title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
articles.summary: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration…
articles.abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

articles.title: Verified Proof Refactoring with Codex and Qwen
articles.summary: We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. A locally served Qwen model uses the…
articles.abstract: We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. A locally served Qwen model uses the open-source Codex CLI to inspect source, retrieve declarations, and test proof replacements. The host keeps a replacement only if it improves the objective and Lean accepts it on every required version. A deterministic CPU pass then refines the verified proofs. On the 60 problems in Lean Refactor Arena, model search achieves a local mean combined score of 82.07, and cleanup raises it to 82.18. The final proofs pass all 127 required proof--version checks. Our system placed first in the open-source LLM track of Lean Refactor Arena at VeriCodeGen.

articles.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
articles.summary: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or…
articles.abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.

articles.title: RVLM-X: Towards a Universal VLM Harness
articles.summary: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them…
articles.abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably plan and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.

articles.title: FN-Prune: Training-Free Expert Pruning with Finite RMSNorm Perturbations
articles.summary: Expert pruning reduces the memory footprint of mixture-of-experts language models, but retaining model quality depends on which experts are removed. Frequency- and magnitude-based scores measure the…
articles.abstract: Expert pruning reduces the memory footprint of mixture-of-experts language models, but retaining model quality depends on which experts are removed. Frequency- and magnitude-based scores measure the expert in isolation and overlook how normalization consumes its contribution: subtracting one expert changes both the direction of the residual stream and the scale applied to what remains. We propose FN-Prune, a training-free criterion that compares the next RMSNorm outputs before and after subtracting each router-weighted expert contribution, holding original routes and weights fixed. Squared differences are averaged over all calibration tokens in one pass; low-scoring experts are physically deleted at uniform per-layer ratios, and inference reroutes among survivors. At 50% expert removal, FN-Prune achieves lower WikiText-2 perplexity than the best published methods on Qwen3, ERNIE, and OLMoE, including a 32% reduction on OLMoE. At the same budget, GSM8K accuracy improves over the best published methods by 7.5 and 7.0 percentage points on Qwen3 and ERNIE, respectively, while multiple-choice gains remain task-dependent.

articles.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
articles.summary: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe…
articles.abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

articles.title: GreenDynaMix: Thermal-Aware Dynamic Mixed-Precision MoE LLM Inference Systems
articles.summary: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload…
articles.abstract: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.

articles.title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
articles.summary: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies.
articles.abstract: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs. On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

articles.title: MOSAIC: Memory-Organized Search with Anti-Imitation Crossover for Training-Free Microarchitecture Optimization
articles.summary: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search.
articles.abstract: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.

articles.title: Normative and neural network models of multisensory integration
articles.summary: Animals continuously detect scents, sights and sounds, which their brains combine into diverse multisensory streams. Multisensory integration accelerates learning, increases reaction speeds and helps…
articles.abstract: Animals continuously detect scents, sights and sounds, which their brains combine into diverse multisensory streams. Multisensory integration accelerates learning, increases reaction speeds and helps to resolve sensory ambiguities. In studying this process, the field has developed a continuum of models; from concise mathematical equations, with a handful of variables, to artificial neural networks, with billions of parameters. In this review, we divide this spectrum into two classes: normative models start from a hypothesis about how multisensory signals should be integrated, while neural network models aim to emulate how circuits could integrate them. Together, these models demonstrate that observers can integrate cues in a statistically optimal fashion, and help to explain experimental findings, including the diversity of multisensory neuron response profiles and network architectures. In this review, we provide a didactic overview of multisensory models, complete with accessible equations and Python code, and compare their assumptions and explanatory power. We detail what has been learned from these models. Finally, we discuss how the ideas and insights from classical theoretical models can be reconciled with those from artificial neural networks, and how this convergence should shape future research.

articles.title: Low-Power Spiking Neural Network Acceleration with Differential Time Representation: A Modular Hardware Framework
articles.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer promising energy efficiency, making them well suited for energy-constrained applications. Much of their energy savings stems from the sparse encoding of spike…
articles.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer promising energy efficiency, making them well suited for energy-constrained applications. Much of their energy savings stems from the sparse encoding of spike trains. We show that spike trains can be represented more efficiently using Differential Time Representation (DTR), which requires fewer bits than Address-Event Representation (AER) or equidistantly sampled 1-bit spike trains. To support multiple input spike trains, we provide a rigorous proof that DTR sequences can be merged with low complexity. We also provide a set of modular hardware streaming components using this representation that can be flexibly connected to construct custom accelerator architectures for specific SNNs. Tailoring the hardware architecture to the selected SNN is streamlined by a Python framework combining the modular hardware components into a full SNN implementation. We use the framework to generate three accelerators for the Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD), Spiking Speech Commands (SSC), and PSMNIST benchmarks, each in a throughput-optimized parallel variant and a resource-reduced time-multiplexed variant. We report results for FPGA and ASIC implementations, the latter synthesized with a fully open-source flow targeting the predictive ASAP7 PDK. On the SHD dataset, the ASIC implementation reaches 92.46% classification accuracy, while sustaining $\approx{}$12,027 inferences per second at 20.37$μ$J per inference, exceeding the neuromorphic Loihi processor by 109$\times$ in throughput and 1.8$\times$ in energy efficiency. The corresponding FPGA implementation achieves $\approx{}$6,023 inferences per second without using DSP blocks. Across all three datasets, the synthesized ASICs reduce energy per inference by 27-37$\times$ relative to their FPGA counterparts, demonstrating that competitive SNN accelerators can be realized entirely within an open-source design flow.

articles.title: Accelerating Dynamic Route Re-solving via Robust Solver Evolution in Automatic Heuristic Design
articles.summary: Multi-goal route planning uses spatial data on service locations and pairwise travel costs to determine a visiting order that minimizes total travel cost. This task can be formulated as the traveling…
articles.abstract: Multi-goal route planning uses spatial data on service locations and pairwise travel costs to determine a visiting order that minimizes total travel cost. This task can be formulated as the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and has benefited from large language model-based automatic heuristic design (AHD) for constructing effective solvers. Despite their effectiveness in static settings, existing methods exhibit substantial re-solving inefficiency when location changes, new requests, or request cancellations alter the underlying request data during execution. Our empirical analysis suggests that ``static-overfitting'' contributes to this inefficiency, as evolved solvers may repeatedly direct search toward overlapping local neighborhoods after dynamic changes. We further find that this ``overfitting'' is associated with limitations in existing evolutionary processes, where lower objective values on some instances coincide with longer solving times. In this paper, we therefore propose ERDR, a plug-and-play framework that integrates two strategies into existing AHD pipelines to guide evolution toward solvers that re-solve dynamically changed instances faster. Specifically, 1) ERDR uses validation-guided reselection to reevaluate candidates on instances excluded from routine evolution, reducing specialization to fixed training instances. 2) ERDR applies runtime robustness-augmented evaluation, supplementing the original evaluation objective of AHD methods with inter-group variability and tail risk in solving time to discourage costly and uneven search. Experiments across multiple TSP scales and dynamic scenarios show that ERDR achieves average re-solving speedups of $2.2\times$ under guided local search and $4.4\times$ under iterated local search.

articles.title: Trading BRAM for LUTs: Hybrid Bit-Level Weight Storage for FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Networks
articles.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive paradigm for energy-efficient AI inference, while their deployment on reconfigurable hardware enables application-specific acceleration without…
articles.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive paradigm for energy-efficient AI inference, while their deployment on reconfigurable hardware enables application-specific acceleration without sacrificing model reprogrammability. However, realizing this potential on FPGAs is often severely constrained by the immense on-chip memory needed to store synaptic weights. Existing compression techniques reduce this storage requirement at the cost of weight precision or accuracy. This work presents a hybrid bit-level weight-storage scheme that trades BRAM capacity for FPGA logic resources while preserving the original weights unmodified. Selected weight bits are implemented using Look-Up Tables (LUTs), while the remaining bits are stored in BRAM and jointly reconstructed during inference. We integrate this approach into a spatial dataflow SNN architecture and introduce a practical bit-mapping heuristic that efficiently partitions weight bits between BRAM and LUT-based logic without modifying the weights. Experimental evaluation demonstrates more than 26% reduction in BRAM utilization with a modest increase in LUT and register usage, resulting in significant overall power savings.

articles.title: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing
articles.summary: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a…
articles.abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. We present HDMark, the first model watermarking framework native to HDC, which encodes ownership in the same hyperdimensional algebra the model computes with. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy. We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.

articles.title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
articles.summary: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs…
articles.abstract: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.

articles.title: SOARS: System One Assisted Reranking for Agentic Search
articles.summary: Deep search agents address complex information needs through iterative retrieval and reasoning, where the relevance of retrieved evidence influences downstream performance. Existing rerankers improve…
articles.abstract: Deep search agents address complex information needs through iterative retrieval and reasoning, where the relevance of retrieved evidence influences downstream performance. Existing rerankers improve retrieval effectiveness but introduce substantial latency and cost when invoked throughout the search trajectory. We introduce SOARS, a training-free framework leveraging a System One model for fast, calibrated relevance estimation. At each search step, SOARS selects query-relevant passages from long documents and reranks candidates in a single call, jointly considering the original question and agent-generated sub-query. Across six LLM backbones on BrowseComp-Plus and WebShaper, SOARS consistently improves answer accuracy and evidence recall while reducing search calls, end-to-end latency, and inference cost. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves GPT-5.4 Mini's accuracy from 73.9% to 84.7% while reducing search calls from 23 to 14, demonstrating the potential of System One reranking for more effective and efficient deep search.

articles.title: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage across Linked LLM Prompts
articles.summary: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a…
articles.abstract: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new, independent view of the same numbers. Since real costs are not public, we measure on synthetic firms with known values how much an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level price and margin statistics, and links a firm's queries. In one prompt, per-field scaling, a fixed-axis instantiation of Zhang et al.'s order-preserving substitution and Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt's released sanitizer keep the attacker's margin-hit advantage over a prior-only guess between -0.6 and +4.4 percentage points. After 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, every disguise we test (Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon\geq 0.5$) has a target recovered significantly more often: under the order-preserving substitution, margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%. The same attacker recovers 29.4 percentage points more margins with fresh maps than with one reused map. Theory explains the contrast: one reused secret bounds all queries by a single full-precision view of the fields shown, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable. Except for Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon=0.5$, the gains persist when the attacker's prior comes from another population model and when values drift by up to 5% between queries; on our firms, whose prose cues are weak, reading the prose with a language model adds at most 2.5 points. Code and data: https://github.com/Jamli58/fresh-keys-stale-secrets

articles.title: From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution
articles.summary: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not…
articles.abstract: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.

articles.title: Is Prosody Encoded in the Neural Audio Codec Mimi?
articles.summary: Neural audio codecs (NACs) have become a fundamental infrastructure for modern speech-language models, discretizing continuous speech signals into token sequences that enable large language models to…
articles.abstract: Neural audio codecs (NACs) have become a fundamental infrastructure for modern speech-language models, discretizing continuous speech signals into token sequences that enable large language models to process and generate audio. Most research evaluates codec quality at the decoding phase, assessing the naturalness of reconstructed speech. However, little research investigates what phonetic information is captured during encoding. In this paper, we investigated the potential correlates of prosody in the NAC Mimi, a codec used by conversational speech agents such as Moshi and Sesame and used in downstream tasks such as speech-to-speech translation (Hibiki).

articles.title: Beyond Fixed-Context Likelihood: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Context Perturbation Discrepancy
articles.summary: The same increase in token log probability from earlier context can be typical at one position and unusually large at another. We introduce Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot…
articles.abstract: The same increase in token log probability from earlier context can be typical at one position and unusually large at another. We introduce Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot detector that measures this gain relative to what a single pretrained language model expects. Keeping the passage fixed, CPD scores each observed token under its full prefix and under a short window of recent tokens. Under the full-prefix distribution, the expected gain equals the KL divergence from that distribution to the restricted-prefix distribution. CPD subtracts this expectation from each observed gain and scales the sum of the signed deviations by its analytical reference standard deviation. On unedited human and AI texts from GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART, subtracting the expected gain raises AUROC by 32.78-35.81 percentage points at the same variance scale. CPD outperforms seven zero-shot baselines, averaging 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate. On original and edited HART passages, the same scores separate texts more clearly by draft origin than by the benchmark's final-expression labels (89.15% versus 65.50% AUROC). Code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-tyf/CPD.

articles.title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages
articles.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such…
articles.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.

articles.title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
articles.summary: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components…
articles.abstract: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. Specifically, we leverage multilingual bias benchmarks in implementing two methods for identifying social bias neurons: activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients. We find the latter method to be more effective, as the neurons it isolates (which are largely concentrated at the model's deepest layers) lead to sharper decreases in model bias when suppressed. Further analysis reveals neuron distribution patterns differ between high- and low-resourced languages, suggesting that a language's representation in pretraining data influences how its biases are represented within model internals. Our results also indicate that neurons linked to gender, nationality, and social class biases overlap the most with neurons related to other bias dimensions, pointing to the pivotal role these three dimensions play in how models learn and handle bias.

articles.title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity
articles.summary: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are…
articles.abstract: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.

articles.title: When "Neutral" Means Irrelevant: A Construct-Validity Audit of NormAd-ETI
articles.summary: NormAd-ETI scores a model's judgment of everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as the cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to a country name. We audit what that three-way…
articles.abstract: NormAd-ETI scores a model's judgment of everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as the cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to a country name. We audit what that three-way score measures. It combines two decisions: whether a supplied norm applies, and whether the action conforms to it. Separating them shows that when only a country is shown, applicability falls to near chance while conformity stays well above it, because the prompt withholds the rule a Neutral label depends on. Because one answer carries both decisions, the score follows the steadier conformity and hides the weaker applicability, and no single prompt recovers the two separately. Dedicated forced-choice probes separate them for frontier models but not for small open models, where the applicability judgment still tracks the hidden acceptability label. Adding a written rationale reduces that conflation without removing it. We recommend reporting the two results separately and measuring the conflation gap.

articles.title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?
articles.summary: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location…
articles.abstract: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at https://github.com/fuji1655/PDC-Bench.

articles.title: Evaluating Latent Knowledge Stability in Multimodal Large Language Models
articles.summary: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational…
articles.abstract: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.

articles.title: Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards
articles.summary: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight…
articles.abstract: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.

articles.title: What If Chinese Were Latinized? A Counterfactual Study of Input Representation, Tokenization, and Language Modeling
articles.summary: If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer.
articles.abstract: If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer. We convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin and train superBPE tokenizers from scratch. The resulting Pinyin vocabularies not only exhibit expected homophone collisions, but also show approximately 10% higher fertility than characters. An alternative BPE configuration changes the relative fertility of the two representations. We further pretrain Llama-style models on Chinese characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall ZhoBLiMP minimal-pair accuracy. An exploratory phonological probe yields near-chance performance for both representations. The broader implication is that written input representations are not merely neutral encodings. Choices for representations affect language modeling and their downstream performances. Latinization never actually happened for Chinese, but other languages did, such as Hangul and Latin script replaced character in Korean and Vietnamese; the cost we measure is a guide to where modeling effort for those languages should concentrate.

articles.title: STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
articles.summary: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student…
articles.abstract: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

articles.title: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
articles.summary: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time…
articles.abstract: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.

articles.title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
articles.summary: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based…
articles.abstract: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

articles.title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
